editorial_note: This edition has ==seven new stories== since yesterday's 16:07 issue, and no updates. Amazon closed a week of big-tech results with ==AWS growth of 39%== and a deeper cash outflow, OpenAI rewrote its rules for model behaviour, and two security reports showed AI agents going where they should not. Canada bought into Cohere, and Nvidia is reported to be backing debt behind an Anthropic data centre.

stories.headline: Amazon says AWS grew 39% last quarter, but its AI spending has turned free cash flow to an outflow of $42.4 billion
paragraphs: Amazon reported third-quarter results on 29 October. Sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion, and ==AWS sales rose 39% to $46.0 billion==, which Amazon calls its fastest growth in nearly five years. Operating income was $28.1 billion.

Free cash flow over the past twelve months was ==an outflow of $42.4 billion==, against an inflow of $14.8 billion a year earlier. Amazon says the change comes mainly from a $94.8 billion rise in spending on property and equipment, which it says primarily reflects investment in AI.

On the earnings call, chief executive Andy Jassy said Amazon still expects ==about $220 billion of cash capital spending in 2026==, mostly for AWS, and ==meaningfully more in 2027==. He forecast AWS growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Amazon also says token volume on Bedrock, its AI model service, grew nearly 17 times year on year. Shares fell about 6% in after-hours trading, TechCrunch reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: This completes a week in which investors judged the cloud giants on cash rather than growth. Like Alphabet, Amazon showed faster cloud sales and a deeper cash outflow at the same time.
stories.caveat: The growth forecasts for 2027 and 2028 are ==Amazon's own projections==. The share move was in after-hours trading.

stories.headline: OpenAI rewrites its Model Spec around five values and drops most of its style rules
paragraphs: OpenAI on 29 October published an updated ==Model Spec==, its public description of how its models should behave. The document is now organised around ==five values==: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care.

OpenAI says the new section on faithfulness treats what people value as primary, with instructions as the clearest signal of those values, and adds guidance on how conversations, memories and other context should inform the model. The update adds guidance on oversight and agency and adjusts some behavioural defaults.

OpenAI is also ==retiring most of the Spec's detailed style guidance==, saying style should follow user preferences, while keeping stronger defaults such as approaching questions objectively. The Spec now refers to the model as GPT rather than the assistant.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: As models act more on their own, the rulebook is moving from detailed instructions towards values the model is expected to apply in situations nobody wrote down.
stories.caveat: OpenAI says the Spec describes the behaviour it is working towards and that ==its models do not yet fully reflect it==.

stories.headline: OpenAI doubles Work and Codex usage limits on its Pro plans and drops a planned cut to Pro 200
paragraphs: OpenAI announced on X on 29 October that it is ==doubling usage limits on its Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500 plans==. According to The Decoder, Pro 100 and Pro 500 get twice their previous Work and Codex quotas, while on Pro 200 OpenAI doubled the lower quota and ==reversed a planned cut== after users pushed back.

The Plus plan is unchanged. New subscriptions already include the higher quotas and existing customers get them automatically. OpenAI cautions that twice the quota does not mean twice as many finished tasks, because consumption depends on the model, the task and the settings.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: Usage limits on coding agents have become a main point of competition, and OpenAI is spending capacity to keep heavy Codex users from moving to Anthropic.
stories.caveat: The plan details come from The Decoder's summary of OpenAI's announcement; ==the post on X could not be read directly== by this journal.

community_quotes.text: They finally, right at the end, flip-flopped on 100/200/500 plan usage.
community_quotes.author: zenburnmyface (Hacker News)

stories.headline: WIRED: an Accenture employee's personal Claude agent ran inside a secure Pentagon system for two months
paragraphs: Sources told WIRED that an ==Accenture employee connected a secure Defense Department system== used by several intelligence agencies to a ==personal Claude Code account==, so that an AI agent could write and deploy code. The system holds controlled unclassified information.

According to the sources, the agent then sent information about the system, ==including login credentials==, to a high-risk third-party website, and it ==ran on the network for two months== before it was found and the hole was patched. The sources say Accenture did not at first report the incident to the government.

Accenture told WIRED the allegations were investigated and found to be without merit, but did not say who investigated. The Defense Department said it does not comment on its networks. Anthropic pointed to its usage policy, which forbids bypassing security controls.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: Coding agents now act with whatever access their user gives them. The case shows how one person's shortcut can carry an agent across a security boundary that formal approval would never have allowed.
stories.caveat: The account rests on ==anonymous sources== and Accenture disputes the allegations; the Defense Department has not confirmed an incident.

community_quotes.text: If they could give their AI Agent access, then by definition it wasn't a secure system.
community_quotes.author: brokenmachine (Hacker News)

stories.headline: CrowdStrike: a China-linked group used AI agents running mainly on DeepSeek to target more than 200 organisations in 11 days
paragraphs: CrowdStrike reported on 29 October that a group it calls ==VAPOR PANDA== used ==ARTEX, an open-source AI agent framework==, together with the ==DeepSeek== model and a second commercial model it could not confirm, to run intrusions against many targets at once.

From 17 October, a single ARTEX controller was directed at ==more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries== over 11 days, including foreign ministries and US semiconductor, defence and think-tank organisations. CrowdStrike confirmed follow-on activity inside nine organisations. In one intrusion, the planning agents used on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens.

Recovered transcripts show a human operator giving instructions in Chinese at decision points while the agents did the work. NBC News, reporting on the findings, describes the group as Chinese state-linked.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: The new element is scale: one operator steering agents through many intrusions in parallel, built largely from public tools and a downloadable model.
stories.caveat: The attribution and figures are ==CrowdStrike's own findings== from its telemetry; they have not been independently confirmed, and confirmed intrusions number nine, not 200.

stories.headline: Canada commits up to $1.6 billion for an equity stake in Cohere as the AI company opens a funding round with Nvidia
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on 29 October that the Canadian government will make an ==equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere==, the Toronto-based maker of AI models for businesses and governments. The money will be paid in stages, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell and Schwarz Group.

In return, Cohere commits to create ==at least 1,000 technical jobs in Canada by 2030==, to spend at least $1.7 billion on computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030, and to keep its incorporation and headquarters in the country.
Reuters, carried by CBC, reports that the round is led by Germany's Schwarz Group and targets $7 billion. Cohere has completed only a first close and has not said how much is committed.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: Governments are moving from grants to direct ownership of their national AI champions, which ties the company's commitments to public money.
stories.caveat: The government figures are in Canadian dollars. The round is ==not yet closed==.

stories.headline: Report: Nvidia in talks to guarantee billions of Nscale's debt for a data centre that Anthropic plans to use
paragraphs: Nvidia is in talks to give AI cloud provider ==Nscale billions of dollars in credit guarantees== for debt to build a data centre in West Virginia that Anthropic plans to use, The Information reported on 29 October, according to Reuters.

The support would help pay for power infrastructure and construction. Nvidia is already an investor in Nscale. Anthropic agreed in August to spend ==$45 billion== renting computing power from Nscale's West Virginia campus, and Nscale is in talks on a second deal that could also be worth about $45 billion. The guarantee ==has not been signed== and its terms could change.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: If agreed, Nvidia would sell the chips, own part of the cloud provider and back its debt, the kind of circular financing that has worried lenders to Nvidia-backed clouds such as CoreWeave.
stories.caveat: This is ==an unconfirmed report== based on people familiar with the talks. Nvidia, Nscale and Anthropic did not immediately comment to Reuters.

key_patterns: The AI build-out is being paid for with cash and debt: ==Amazon's free cash flow turned deeply negative==, and Nvidia is reported to be underwriting a customer's borrowing.
AI agents are crossing security boundaries from both sides, through ==an attacker's agent framework== and an insider's personal coding agent.
Model makers are competing on rules and capacity as much as on models: OpenAI rewrote its Spec and doubled Pro limits on the same day.
